# Diagnostics export plan

Goal: `zenith diagnostics` can hand a machine readable health report to the monitoring stack.

## Checklist

- [ ] `--format json|text` flag on `zenith health` (default text)
- [ ] Stable JSON schema, versioned (`schema_version`)
- [ ] Prometheus text exposition at `zenith health --format prom`
- [ ] TLS certificate verification summary per node (expiry, issuer, days left)
- [ ] 5 second timeout flag, default from config
- [ ] Integration test per format
- [ ] Document the schema in docs/health-schema.md

## Order of work

1. JSON first: everything else builds on the same `HealthReport` struct.
2. Prometheus is a different rendering of the same struct, no new probes.
3. TLS verification adds probes, so it goes last behind its own flag.

Fixed. The limiter tests pass (10 of 10, including the new regression test) and clippy is clean with `-D warnings`.

**Root cause:** `Limiter::merge_remote` computed `min(local, remote) + pending_refund` and stored it without the capacity clamp that `Bucket::refill` applies. After a long idle gap the bucket was already full, so any pending refund pushed it past the burst. Only replicas that sync with Redis call `merge_remote`, which is why single replicas looked fine.

```rust
let merged = self.tokens.min(remote_tokens) + self.pending_refund;
self.tokens = merged.min(self.capacity as f64);
```

The public API did not change. One thing I did not touch: `refund` itself still lets `pending_refund` grow without bound if `merge_remote` is never called on a replica. That is harmless now that the merge clamps, but a cap there would be tidier if you want it as a follow-up.

Profile the memory allocator churn in the batch runner of the parquet zero-copy deserializer. Throughput dropped about 18% after the dictionary page work and I suspect we allocate per chunk again. Find it, fix it if it is what I think, and show me numbers before and after.
I'll read the batch runner first, then measure allocations with the DHAT profile build so we are not guessing.

Confirmed by reading: `buf` is created inside the innermost loop, so every chunk allocates, grows and frees a `Vec<u8>`. The bench already reuses a `scratch` buffer, which is why the bench never showed the regression. Let me measure the real runner.

262,412 allocations for 4,096 row groups of 64 chunks: one per chunk, plus growth reallocations inside `decode_into`. 1.48 GB of allocator traffic to move 16 million rows. The fix is a single scratch buffer for the whole run, cleared per chunk so the capacity is kept.
`RunnerOptions` already has `max_chunk_bytes` (1 MiB default), a good starting capacity. Rebuilding and measuring again.

Allocations dropped from 262,412 to 1,972 and throughput rose from 4.80M to 5.87M rows/s (+22%). There are still ~1,970 allocations, which is more than one buffer should need, so something else allocates. Looking at the dictionary decode path.

`materialize` copies every dictionary value into its own `Vec` and then concatenates them: two copies and an allocation per value. This is the zero-copy deserializer, so it should write straight from the dictionary slice into `out`.

Done, and the numbers are clear:

| | allocations | throughput |
|---|---|---|
| before | 262,412 | 4.80M rows/s |
| scratch buffer only | 1,972 | 5.87M rows/s |
| plus dictionary fix | 7 | 7.09M rows/s |

Two separate causes:
1. `BatchRunner::run` created a fresh `Vec<u8>` for every chunk. It now reuses one buffer, cleared between chunks.
2. `DictPage::materialize` staged each value in its own `Vec` before concatenating. It now copies straight from the dictionary slice.

```rust
out.reserve(indices.len() * self.avg_value_len());
for &i in indices {
    out.extend_from_slice(self.lookup(i)?);
}
```

That is a 48% throughput gain over the regressed build, and about 18% better than before the dictionary work, which matches your suspicion. All 31 reader tests pass. I did not add a benchmark guard for allocations; a DHAT assertion in CI would stop this regressing again, if you want it.

`zenith cluster ping` reports healthy nodes in the eu-west zone as timed out. Those links are 400 ms away and our timeout is a fixed 500 ms, so the distributed consensus ping fails whenever there is a little jitter. Make the timeout adapt to the link.
I'll read the ping implementation and where the 500 ms comes from.
The timeout is a constant passed straight through. I'll plan the change so the quorum logic stays untouched.

The distributed consensus ping now adapts to the link, and all 10 tests pass (the slow-link test failed first, which is how I found the cold-start problem).

- `RttEstimate` keeps a smoothed round trip (`srtt = 7/8 srtt + 1/8 sample`, as TCP does) per node for the whole ping run.
- The timeout is `max(base, 3 x srtt)`. With no sample yet it is `4 x base`, so a healthy node 600 ms away answers its first ping and seeds the estimate.
- A dead node still times out, just after 2 s the first time instead of 500 ms; the failover tests confirm it is reported dead.

```rust
let est = estimates.entry(node.name.clone()).or_default();
let r = ping_node(node.addr, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, est);
```

Trade-off to be aware of: a one-shot `zenith cluster ping` against a dead node now waits up to 2 seconds on that node. If that feels slow for scripts, we can cap the cold-start multiplier with a `--cold-timeout` flag.
